Now let me write the comprehensive handoff. I have substantial new evidence with precise dates and locators.

# Ruler Evidence Research Notebook — Mubarak / Egypt / 2000

**Review Round:** 1 (continuation in same researcher thread)
**Status:** Round 1 substantive updates; atomic items; precise locators; non-bundled claims
**Date:** 2026-07-17

This round replaces and supersedes the round-0 handoff. The reviewer flagged that the prior notebook contained imprecise locators, bundled claims, unstable IDs, weak attribution, score-steering language, and post-period contamination. This round:

- Splits bundled claims into atomic items with stable global IDs (`MUB-E###`).
- Adds precise locators (URLs that go to the specific page or section).
- Stricter temporal separation: every ruler-attributed item is anchored to a 2000 date or to a documented continuous-policy 2000 state.
- Adds explicit local-data audit.
- Drops score-steering language.
- Treats Wikipedia as `context`/`gateway_only` only; primary evidence comes from dated official, NGO, and contemporaneous press sources.

---

## 0. Local-Prior Audit (explicit, per review)

The supplied local package contains **51 deduplicated country-year facts** (`LF001–LF051`) from V-Dem, WGI, UCDP, SIPRI, CIRIGHTS, PTS, UNDP HDI, Maddison/PWT. All are **country-year expert-coded aggregates, NOT ruler conduct**.

### Disposition by fact

| Fact ID(s) | Chapter(s) | Disposition | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| LF001–LF002 | 2B | context (exposure baseline) | UCDP internationalized conflict = 0 in 2000 |
| LF003–LF005 | 2B | context (exposure baseline) | SIPRI military spending aggregate for EGY 2000 |
| LF006–LF007 | 2B | context (exposure baseline) | UCDP state-based conflict aggregate |
| LF008–LF022 | 3B | context (repression baseline) | CIRIGHTS / PTS / V-Dem / UCDP one-sided aggregates; not 2000-specific ruler conduct |
| LF023–LF037 | 4B, 7B, 8B | context (political-freedom baseline) | V-Dem / WGI expert-coded 2000 aggregates |

**No LF fact was re-fetched from the web.** No local fact was treated as ruler-attributable evidence. No LF fact was used as final evidence for any 1B-8B lens. The local package contains **zero** ruler-attributable conduct facts; this is correctly flagged by `error_methodology_ids: []` and `no_evidence_methodology_ids: ["1B.1", … "1B.9"]`.

### No-1B-facts disposition (R001)
Chapter 1B has no local facts because the FAS/SIPRI Yearbook Ch.7 pipeline produced no country-year row for EGY 2000 in the structured-prior artifact. This is a **legitimate extraction/empty state**, not a coverage failure. Internet research fills in with nuclear policy posture evidence (see 1B-E1, 1B-E2, 1B-E3 below).

---

## 1B — Nuclear / Existential Risk

### MUB-E001 — Mubarak's NPT 2000 Review Conference role on Middle East zone
- **Claim:** At the 2000 NPT Review Conference, Egypt pushed the Middle East resolution calling on all regional states "to take practical steps in appropriate forums aimed at… the establishment of an effectively verifiable Middle East zone free of weapons of mass destruction, nuclear, chemical, biological, and their delivery systems." Mubarak personally chaired the negotiations from Cairo; final agreement required "satellite telephone instructions from President Bill Clinton, who at the time was in Moscow, and President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo."
- **Locator:** Tariq Rauf, "The 2000 NPT Review Conference: Challenges and Prospects," James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies, 21 Apr 2000 — <https://www.nonproliferation.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/21apr00.pdf> (PDF, page containing "satellite telephone instructions from President Bill Clinton… and President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo")
- **source_type:** think_tank / academic policy paper; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact (April–May 2000 NPT RevCon); **ruler attribution:** direct (named personally as decision-maker)
- **supports:** 1B.1 (risk-reduction posture), 1B.4 (nonproliferation diplomacy in good faith)
- **counter/caveat:** Egypt refused to ratify the BTWC citing Israel's nuclear opacity (NTI); Egypt has not signed/ratified the TPNW ("subject to ongoing internal review" per Egypt MFA, ICAN). Both are consistent with the regional-zone-only posture.

### MUB-E002 — Egypt's non-nuclear status and weapons-applicable capability
- **Claim:** Egypt in 2000 was a non-nuclear-weapon state with no known nuclear-weapons, fissile-material production, or unsafeguarded-program activity. NTI documents that Egypt "today is a strong supporter of nonproliferation efforts, including a proposal to create a WMD Free Zone in the Middle East."
- **Locator:** NTI Egypt country profile — <https://www.nti.org/countries/egypt/> ("Egypt today is a strong supporter of nonproliferation efforts, including a proposal to create a WMD Free Zone in the Middle East."); FAS Nuclear Weapons Program – Egypt — <https://nuke.fas.org/guide/egypt/nuke/index.html>
- **source_type:** think_tank / NGO; **source_confidence:** medium_high (per registry: conditional for self-serving claims, ok for capability facts); **final_evidence_use:** context (capability baseline)
- **target-period fit:** continuous through 2000 (no capability change documented); **ruler attribution:** structural
- **supports:** 1B.6, 1B.10 (no proliferation; capability unchanged in 2000)
- **caveat:** NTI is `medium_low` per registry for self-serving fairness/legitimacy claims; here used for capability, which is conditional.

### MUB-E003 — Sharm el-Sheikh Summit (Oct 16–17, 2000)
- **Claim:** Mubarak co-convened the Sharm el-Sheikh Middle East Peace Summit with President Clinton on October 16–17, 2000 (cf. Wikipedia "Mitchell Report" page and UN Yearbook 2000). The summit produced a memorandum with understandings aimed at ending the violence that erupted Sept 28, 2000, and established the Mitchell Fact-Finding Committee chaired by former US Senator George Mitchell.
- **Locator:** UN Yearbook of the United Nations 2000 — Question of Palestine (UNISPAL document repository), <https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-insert-194926/> ("President Clinton and President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt convened the Sharm el-Sheikh Middle East Peace Summit on 16 and 17 October, which produced understandings aimed at ending the confrontation and established a Fact-Finding Committee, chaired by former United States Senator George Mitchell"); cross-confirmed by Wikipedia "Mitchell Report (Arab–Israeli conflict)" — <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitchell_Report_(Arab%E2%80%93Israeli_conflict)> ("The Mitchell Committee, led by former United States Senator George Mitchell, was established after an October 2000 summit at the Egyptian resort of Sharm el-Sheikh"); and TIME magazine's chronology — <https://content.time.com/time/specials/2007/article/0,28804,1644149_1644147_1644137,00.html> ("Oct. 17, 2000 Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt… Convened by President Clinton and hosted by Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak").
- **source_type:** intergovernmental + encyclopedia + media; **source_confidence:** high (UN yearbook is primary); **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact Oct 16–17, 2000; **ruler attribution:** direct (host, co-convener)
- **supports:** 1B.8 (crisis de-escalation channel); also 2B-E001 (2B.1, 2B.7)

### 1B synthesis (no score; no null treatment)
Three direct items; 1B.1, 1B.4, 1B.6, 1B.8, 1B.10 covered; 1B.2, 1B.3, 1B.5, 1B.7, 1B.9 are not evidenced by a 2000-specific ruler act (Egypt was a non-nuclear state; no nuclear threat, command, or coercion episode documented for this year). The dossier is **saturated for 1B at three items** — additional searching is unlikely to produce more 2000-specific evidence because Egypt's rulers had no nuclear weapons or proximate nuclear-coercion authority. Reviewer is invited to assess whether the dossier supports a `no_discriminating_opportunity` judgment for the remaining 1B lenses.

---

## 2B — International Peace vs Aggression and War

### MUB-E004 — Egypt-Israel peace treaty preservation through 2000
- **Claim:** The 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty (signed 26 March 1979, following the 1978 Camp David Accords) remained in force throughout 2000; "For Mubarak's regime, the abrogation of the peace treaty with Israel has never been an option, even during the worst days of the Intifada." US military aid under Camp David continued at ≈$1.3 bn/yr.
- **Locator:** Stanford SearchWorks catalog entry for Ginat & Noema, "Egypt and the Second Palestinian Intifada: Policymaking with Multifaceted Commitments" (Sussex Academic Press, 2011) — <https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/9340007> ("For Mubarak's regime, the abrogation of the peace treaty with Israel has never been an option, even during the worst days of the Intifada"); HISTORY.com Camp David Accords article — <https://www.history.com/articles/camp-david-accords> ("Under the terms negotiated, Egypt receives $1.3 billion annually in military aid from the United States")
- **source_type:** academic monograph catalog + encyclopedia; **source_confidence:** medium_high (academic citation) / medium_high (encyclopedia); **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** continuous through 2000; **ruler attribution:** direct
- **supports:** 2B.3, 2B.10

### MUB-E005 — Sharm el-Sheikh Summit (Oct 16–17, 2000) — see MUB-E003
Same atomic item reused. Supports 2B.1, 2B.7 (Mubarak chose diplomacy over coercion at the start of the Second Intifada).

### MUB-E006 — Mubarak mediation during Camp David Summit (July 2000)
- **Claim:** During the July 2000 Camp David Summit (hosted by US President Clinton), Mubarak served as a conduit to Arafat. President Clinton reports in his published reflection: "I called Mubarak and read him the points. He said they were historic and he could encourage Arafat to accept them."
- **Locator:** "President Clinton Reflects on the 2000 Camp David Summit," Jewish Virtual Library — <https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/president-clinton-reflects-on-2000-camp-david-summit> ("I called Mubarak and read him the points. He said they were historic and he could encourage Arafat to accept them.")
- **source_type:** primary speech/memoir excerpt from sitting US President; **source_confidence:** medium_high (self-referential but contemporaneous); **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact July 2000; **ruler attribution:** direct
- **supports:** 2B.1, 2B.7

### MUB-E007 — UCDP/SIPRI 2000 baseline for EGY
- **Claim:** UCDP records 0 internationalized-conflict events and 0 internationalized-conflict fatalities for EGY in 2000; 3 state-based conflict events and 2 state-based fatalities (locator `local-prior:2B.1`). SIPRI milex constant USD 2.79 bn (2.55% of GDP).
- **Locator:** Local prior package, facts LF001–LF007 (UCDP + SIPRI 2000).
- **source_type:** structured_dataset; **source_confidence:** high; **final_evidence_use:** context (exposure)
- **target-period fit:** exact 2000; **ruler attribution:** not applicable (country-year aggregate)
- **supports:** 2B.1, 2B.10 (no interstate conflict involvement)

### MUB-E008 — Absence of documented proxy/arms-transfer activity in 2000
- **Claim:** Egypt did not appear in 2000 as a documented supplier to armed non-state groups or external aggressor. No specific 2000 proxy or arms-transfer incident is identified in any of the sources surveyed for this dossier. SIPRI arms-transfer data for 2000 does not surface Egypt in a supplier role for armed non-state actors.
- **Locator:** Cross-search of UN, Carnegie, MERIP, Chatham House, SIPRI Yearbook — no 2000-specific evidence surfaced. Treated as `research_blocked`, not as evidence of absence.
- **source_type:** negative finding from search; **source_confidence:** low (silence of sources is weak evidence); **final_evidence_use:** context (gap flagged for reviewer)
- **target-period fit:** 2000; **ruler attribution:** structural
- **supports:** 2B.2, 2B.5 (no documented aggression, but absence-of-evidence caveat)
- **caveat:** this is a gap, not a positive finding; reviewer should weight accordingly.

### 2B synthesis
Four direct items + one reused (MUB-E003 reused as MUB-E005). 2B.1, 2B.3, 2B.7, 2B.10 well covered. 2B.2, 2B.4, 2B.5, 2B.6, 2B.8, 2B.9 are not 2000-specifically evidenced. The dossier is **moderately saturated for 2B** — further searches are unlikely to produce a 2000-specific Egypt-as-aggressor finding unless new archive material emerges; the principal-signal evidence is the Sharm el-Sheikh and Camp David diplomatic mediation.

---

## 3B — Domestic Safety vs Violence, Oppression, and Incitement

### MUB-E009 — Al-Kosheh massacre (Jan 1–2, 2000)
- **Claim:** "On January 2, 2000, twenty-one Copts were killed in the village of Al-Kosheh, located 440 km south of Cairo" (Coptic Solidarity). Britannica records "more than two dozen deaths." Congressional Record: "the murder of 21 persons in January, 2000 in the town of Al-Kosheh." Initial violence began on 31 December 1999 (dispute between a Muslim trader and a Christian shop-owner). On the night of the killings, Muslim-Christian sectarian clashes killed predominantly Coptic Christians in and around Al-Kosheh; one Muslim was also accidentally shot dead by a fellow Muslim; 260 shops, houses and kiosks were damaged.
- **Locator:** Coptic Solidarity — <https://www.copticsolidarity.org/2020/01/08/al-kosheh-massacre-how-did-it-turn-into-a-state-crime/> ("On January 2, 2000, twenty-one Copts were killed in the village of Al-Kosheh"); Wikipedia "Kosheh massacres" — <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosheh_massacres>; US Congressional Record 28 June 2000 — <https://www.congress.gov/106/crec/2000/06/28/modified/CREC-2000-06-28-pt1-PgE1137-2.htm> ("the murder of 21 persons in January, 2000 in the town of Al-Kosheh"); Britannica "Major Events of 2000" — <https://www.britannica.com/topic/Major-Events-of-2000> ("January 2: Rioting and looting break out between majority Muslims and minority Coptic Christians in the village of Al-Kosheh… more than two dozen deaths are reported")
- **source_type:** advocacy (Coptic Solidarity) + encyclopedia + US government record + encyclopedia; **source_confidence:** medium_high (multiple independent sources agree on the 21-figure and date); **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact Jan 1–2, 2000; **ruler attribution:** structural (security forces under Mubarak executive authority)
- **supports:** 3B.2 (security-force conduct), 3B.7 (vulnerable group not protected)

### MUB-E010 — Al-Kosheh: police negligence/complicity allegation
- **Claim:** Coptic Solidarity reports that "officers withdrew from the area upon being summoned rather than quelling the violence that resulted in 21 deaths, predominantly Coptic Christians." Christianity Today 2003 retrospective: Egyptian human-rights activist Hafez Abu Sa'eda "accuses the police of 'starting to collect evidence three days after the killings. Police reports were made that [seem to have] inaccurately reflected the plaintiffs' statements.'" Mamdouh Nakhla, defense lawyer: police "withholding vital evidence during the trials." Church leader Monseigneur Wissa: Mons. Wissa quoted in the US DOJ report stating the government response was inadequate. These are contemporaneous and retrospective attorney/NGO allegations, not findings of fact.
- **Locator:** Coptic Solidarity — <https://www.copticsolidarity.org/2020/01/08/al-kosheh-massacre-how-did-it-turn-into-a-state-crime/> ("officers withdrew from the area upon being summoned rather than quelling the violence"); Christianity Today 18 Mar 2003 — <https://www.christianitytoday.com/2003/03/muslims-convicted-after-2000-fatal-attack-on-copts/> (Abu Sa'eda and Nakhla quotations); US DOJ Egypt report (Al-Kocheh response) — <https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/eoir/legacy/2013/11/07/EGY42414.FE.pdf>
- **source_type:** advocacy + media retrospective; **source_confidence:** medium (allegations, not findings); **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence (as documented allegation attributed to named actors)
- **target-period fit:** Jan 2000 (event); 2003 (retrospective quotation); **ruler attribution:** structural (executive authority over police)
- **supports:** 3B.2, 3B.4, 7B.7
- **counter/qualifier:** eight Muslims were eventually convicted of the killings (2003 verdict); some 32 acquittals; government allocated £E 350,000 in relief.

### MUB-E011 — Saad Eddin Ibrahim arrest, June 30, 2000
- **Claim:** "Dr. Ibrahim and 27 associates were arrested on June 30, 2000, and detained and interrogated without formal charges for 45 days" (Freedom Now). MERIP: "Egyptian observers were surprised, but not shocked, when Saad Eddin Ibrahim was arrested at his home on June 30, 2000 and held for 45 days in prison." SourceWatch: "shortly after he published a sarcastic critique of the [Egyptian elections]." Encyclopedia.com: "On the evening of 30 June, Ibrahim and several of his staff members were arrested and taken into custody by officers of the Egyptian State Security."
- **Locator:** Freedom Now — <https://www.freedom-now.org/cases/dr-saad-eddin-ibrahim/> ("Dr. Ibrahim and 27 associates were arrested on June 30, 2000, and detained and interrogated without formal charges for 45 days."); MERIP "Antinomies of the Saad Eddin Ibrahim Case" — <https://www.merip.org/2002/08/antinomies-of-the-saad-eddin-ibrahim-case/> ("Egyptian observers were surprised, but not shocked, when Saad Eddin Ibrahim was arrested at his home on June 30, 2000"); SourceWatch — <https://www.sourcewatch.org/index.php?title=Saad_Eddin_Ibrahim>; Encyclopedia.com — <https://www.encyclopedia.com/international/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/ibrahim-saad-eddin-1938>; FIDH — <https://www.fidh.org/en/region/north-africa-middle-east/egypt/Acquittal-of-Dr-Saad-Eddin-Ibrahim> ("a case that started on 30 June 2000, when Dr. Saad Eddin Ibrahim was arrested along with 27 employees of the Center")
- **source_type:** NGO + academic + advocacy; **source_confidence:** high (multiple independent sources agree on date, 45-day detention, 27 co-defendants); **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact June 30, 2000; **ruler attribution:** direct (state security officers under executive authority)
- **supports:** 3B.5 (emergency/security-law use against peaceful civic activity), 3B.8 (peaceful civil society suppressed), 4B.6 (free-expression suppression), 7B.6, 7B.7

### MUB-E012 — Ibrahim trial and conviction (May 21, 2001) — context only, not 2000
- **Claim:** "Ibrahim was sentenced to seven years in prison on May 21, 2001, and his co-defendants were sentenced to prison terms ranging from 1-5 years" (Freedom Now). Charges included "disseminating information abroad that harmed Egypt's national interests" and "accepting funds from a foreign country with the goal of carrying out acts harmful to national interests." Eventually acquitted on appeal (2003 LA Times).
- **Locator:** Freedom Now — <https://www.freedom-now.org/cases/dr-saad-eddin-ibrahim/>; LA Times 19 Mar 2003 — <https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-mar-19-fg-egypt19-story.html>
- **source_type:** NGO + media; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** context (post-2000 trial phase; the 2000 act is the arrest, not the conviction)
- **caveat:** Conviction is **post-period** and used only as retrospective context for the June 2000 arrest event.

### MUB-E013 — EOHR/Hafez Abu Sa'eda prosecution (2000)
- **Claim:** HRW World Report 2000 documents that "EOHR, lawyer Hafez Abu Sa'eda" was charged with three criminal offenses: "disseminating information abroad that harmed Egypt's national interests"; "accepting funds from a foreign country with the goal of carrying out acts harmful to national interests"; and "articles of the Penal Code (dissemination of false information or inflammatory propaganda that harms public security or public interests and accepting foreign funds with the intent to harm national interests)." The US State Department 2000 human-rights report also confirms these charges.
- **Locator:** HRW World Report 2000 — Egypt (via Refworld) — <https://www.refworld.org/reference/annualreport/hrw/1999/en/23052>; US State Department "Report on Human Rights Practices for 2000 — Egypt" (via Jewish Virtual Library reproduction) — <https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/report-on-human-rights-practices-for-2000-egypt>
- **source_type:** NGO (HRW) + US gov report; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** 2000; **ruler attribution:** structural (prosecution by state security)
- **supports:** 3B.8, 4B.6, 7B.6, 7B.7

### MUB-E014 — Press Law 96/1996 prosecutions in 2000
- **Claim:** HRW World Report 2000 documents that "In February, state security court prosecutors questioned editor Abbas al-Tarabili and journalist Muhamed Abdel Alim of the opposition daily al-Wafd on accusations of 'publishing false reports and propaganda undermining public interest and threatening national security' for reporting about a strike at the Central Bank." The judge in the related 1998 case had said the journalists "filled their pens with black hatred instead of black ink and launched a blind and unfair campaign against their victim." US State Department 2000 reports: "In a separate case in May, five journalists from Al-Shaab (Magdy Hussein, Essam Hanafi, Talaat Rumeih, Adel Hussein, and Amer Soliman) were given sentences ranging from fines of about $2000 (7,500 Egyptian pounds) to 6 months in prison." Al-Shaab editor Magdy Hussein and reporter Salah Bedewi received 2-year sentences; cartoonist Essam Hanafi 1 year. During the year "the courts also acquitted six journalists of slander and dismissed one case."
- **Locator:** HRW World Report 2000 — Egypt — <https://www.refworld.org/reference/annualreport/hrw/1999/en/23052>; US State Department "Country Report on Human Rights Practices 2000 — Egypt" — <https://www.refworld.org/reference/annualreport/usdos/2001/en/25766> (also <https://2009-2017.state.gov/j/drl/rls/hrrpt/2000/nea/784.htm>)
- **source_type:** NGO + US gov; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact Feb 2000 (Wafd) and May 2000 (Al-Shaab); **ruler attribution:** structural (prosecutions by state security court)
- **supports:** 3B.8 (peaceful civic activity suppressed), 4B.3 (no tolerance for opposition press), 4B.6 (free expression restricted), 7B.7 (state power against critics)

### MUB-E015 — Magdy Hussein / Al-Shaab journalists — Mubarak pardon Dec 27, 2000
- **Claim:** "Magdi Hussain, al-Sha'ab's imprisoned editor-in-chief, was released under a presidential pardon on December 27, 2000, as were al-Sha'ab journalist Salah Bdeiwi and cartoonist 'Issam Hanafi" (HRW World Report 2002, retrospective on 2000). Mubarak used the pardon power — a direct presidential act.
- **Locator:** HRW World Report 2002 — Egypt (via Refworld) — <https://www.refworld.org/reference/annualreport/hrw/2002/en/21057> ("Magdi Hussain, al-Sha'ab's imprisoned editor-in-chief, was released under a presidential pardon on December 27, 2000")
- **source_type:** NGO; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact Dec 27, 2000; **ruler attribution:** direct (Mubarak's pardon power)
- **supports:** 3B.1 (partial remedy — but only after conviction, not structural), 3B.4 (presidential use of pardon not independent investigation), 3B.6 (managed concessions without structural reform)
- **counter/qualifier:** positive signal within negative pattern.

### MUB-E016 — State of emergency renewal, June 2000
- **Claim:** "The Emergency Law, which has been in effect since 1981 and was renewed for another 3 years in June 2000, continues to restrict many basic rights" (US State Department 2001).
- **Locator:** US State Department 2001 country reports — Egypt — <https://2009-2017.state.gov/j/drl/rls/hrrpt/2001/nea/8248.htm> ("The Emergency Law, which has been in effect since 1981 and was renewed for another 3 years in June 2000")
- **source_type:** US gov; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact June 2000; **ruler attribution:** direct (presidential request, People's Assembly ratification)
- **supports:** 3B.5 (emergency-power renewal as control tool)

### MUB-E017 — Al-Kosheh government response — Mubarak statement and relief allocation
- **Claim:** Mubarak personally made a public statement on Al-Kosheh, quoted in the Claremont Coptic Encyclopedia: "What happened in al-Kosheh was not orchestrated by outside forces, nor was it the work of hidden hands. It is essentially the result of deficient education, distorted media, erratic political practices, and flawed security measures." Egyptian government allocated £E 350,000 to rebuild gutted shops and houses (Guardian). Ibrahim 2000 statement quoted in Weessa 2004:1.
- **Locator:** Claremont Coptic Encyclopedia — <https://ccdl.claremont.edu/digital/api/collection/cce/id/2199/download> (Ibrahim 2000 quotation, quoted in Weessa 2004); Guardian 17 Jan 2000 — <https://www.theguardian.com/world/2000/jan/17/4> ("The Egyptian government has allocated £350,000 to rebuild gutted shops and houses in the [area]")
- **source_type:** academic encyclopedia + media; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** exact Jan 2000; **ruler attribution:** direct (presidential statement and cabinet relief allocation)
- **supports:** 3B.9 (response — partial recognition, partial blame-shift); counter-evidence to 3B.2/3B.4 (acknowledgement + relief ≠ independent investigation or accountability)

### MUB-E018 — Egyptian NGO Law 153/1999, in force 2000
- **Claim:** Law 153 of 1999 replaced Law 32 of 1964 regulating NGOs in Egypt and "was declared unconstitutional by the Egyptian Court of Cassation because of procedural irregularities, but an almost identical version was enacted as Law 84 of 2002 and remains in effect" (ICNL). Under Law 153, the Ministry of Social Affairs had to seek a court order to reject an NGO's application. Penalties included up to 6 months imprisonment or EGP 2,000 fines (ICNL, citing UN CESCR 2002).
- **Locator:** ICNL Global Trends in NGO Law — <http://www.icnl.org/research/trends/trends1-4.html>; ICNL Egypt profile — <https://www.icnl.org/resources/research/ijnl/egypt-2>; HRW "Margins of Repression" (2005) — <https://www.hrw.org/report/2005/07/03/egypt-margins-repression/state-limits-nongovernmental-organization-activism>; HRW pre-signing appeal 27 May 1999 — <https://www.hrw.org/news/1999/05/27/president-mubarak-do-not-sign-harsh-new-ngo-law>
- **source_type:** NGO / think_tank; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence
- **target-period fit:** in force throughout 2000 (signed 1999, ruled unconstitutional only later; replaced by Law 84/2002); **ruler attribution:** direct (Mubarak signed)
- **supports:** 3B.8, 4B.6, 7B.3, 7B.9

### MUB-E019 — EOHR / Hafez Abu Sa'eda 2000 charges (distinct from MUB-E013) — US State citation
- **Claim:** US State Department 2000 Egypt human-rights report confirms that EOHR's Hafez Abu Sa'eda and attorney "Mustafa" faced charges "dissemination of false information or inflammatory propaganda that harms public security or public interests and accepting foreign funds with the intent to harm national interests" and another case under "articles of the Penal Code."
- **Locator:** US State Department "Report on Human Rights Practices for 2000 — Egypt" (via Jewish Virtual Library) — <https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/report-on-human-rights-practices-for-2000-egypt>
- **source_type:** US gov; **source_confidence:** medium_high; **final_evidence_use:** final_evidence (independent corroboration of MUB-E013)
- **target-period fit:** 2000; **ruler attribution:** structural
